speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More than four years ago, I said in this House that, "Food waste is a serious and growing problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, some Singaporeans struggle to have three meals a day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both problems can be alleviated if we introduce a Good Samaritan Food Donation Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This piece of legislation would help encourage companies and organisations to donate healthy food that would otherwise go to waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will help both the environment and our people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry of Environment and Water Resources support a Private Member's Bill for a Good Samaritan Food Donation Act?" Four years later, I am glad and excited that we are now ready to move the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Honestly, I am really hiding my pure excitement and uncontrollable happiness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill has been made possible by the tremendous work done by the Good Samaritan Legislation Review Committee over the past four years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Committee comprise of representatives from BreadTalk, DBS bank, Food from the Heart, Foodscape Collective, Mandarin Oriental Singapore, NTUC Fairprice, Restaurant Association of Singapore, the Singapore Youth for Climate Action, the Food Bank, the Fullerton Hotels and Resorts, Ya Kun International and my legislative assistants, grassroot leaders and fellow Members of Parliament, Ms Poh Li San, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Edward Chia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been a privilege working with this team of passionate volunteers who donated their time and energy, so that many people and our planet can benefit from this piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We spent hours, days, weeks, months and years discussing what should and should not be included in the Bill, what food should be covered and who should be covered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We consulted extensively, conducting public consultations and meeting with restaurants, hotels, social enterprises, primary food producers, the food processing sector, distributors, wholesalers, food logistic, transport and delivery provider companies, supermarkets and merchants, bakeries and non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am grateful for the Committee's hard work and inspired by their passion in wanting to help others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a Bill by the people, for the people and for our planet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have waited a long time to say this, Mr.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Louis Ng, I can see the excitement in your words.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Orders of the Day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have to say first, that sometimes people do not like having a meal with me because I constantly nag them about not wasting food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I will sometimes join a table of people who are already eating and they will say, “Louis is here, cannot waste food already”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I secretly quite like this when they say that because tackling food wastage is something very close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I constantly tell them, “Do not waste food, take what you can eat and finish eating what you have already taken”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More than four years ago, I was at a buffet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just as we were finishing our meal, my daughter, Ella, and I saw perfectly edible food being thrown away right before our eyes, because the buffet had ended.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An entire cake, freshly brought out not long ago and missing just the slice, was dumped into a trash bag.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As parents, we always tell our children not to waste food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I could not explain to Ella why we were now seeing good food being thrown away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke to the restaurant and asked if the food could be donated instead of being dumped or being wasted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reply was that they were worried about liability issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I offered to sign a waiver of liability and even offered to bring the food to distribute to families in Yishun, families struggling to have three meals a day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even then, the restaurant refused to donate the food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not all liability can be waived and the uncertainty of legal proceedings can be a huge business risk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It pains me to say this, but it can be easier to just throw food away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More than four years after this meal, I stand here before this House with the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is only possible thanks to the amazing and collaborative work done by the Good Samaritan Legislation Review Committee over the past four years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We consulted extensively, holding public consultations and meeting with restaurants, hotels, social enterprises, primary food producers, food processing companies, distributors, wholesalers, food logistics, transport and delivery provider companies, supermarkets and merchants, bakeries and non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first public consultation was conducted through an online survey from 30 July 2021 to 12 September 2021.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We also held several extensive focus group discussions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On 4 April 2024, the Committee conducted the second public consultation, where we presented the draft Bill to members of the public and seek their inputs and feedback.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We scrutinised and debated every clause of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We revised the draft Bill after the second public consultation to address all the feedback we received.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Where we were not able to incorporate the feedback, we explained why to the public and the various stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this Second Reading, in addition to responding to my fellow Members’ questions, I will also respond to additional feedback we received from members of the public and other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is the work of many people who have shared their views, suggestions and feedback, and I am immensely grateful for the important role they played in shaping this important piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have a serious food waste problem in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should be concerned about this astounding wastage for four reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More than 90% of our food supply has to be imported.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the mercy of global trade winds, we have to fight harder than most countries to put food on our tables.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When we waste food, we undermine this fight.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can do the math – 750,000 tonnes of annual food waste divided by 1.6 million tonnes of commonly consumed food imported annually.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It could be that nearly half of our most commonly consumed food imports go into our trash, not our stomachs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have to spend so much more and work so much harder because of our food waste habits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second reason to care about food waste is the strain it puts on our waste disposal system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we incinerate food we do not eat, we will still have to find space to store the ashes left behind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no second landfill waiting for us.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must reduce the problem of food waste if we are to have a chance of prolonging the lifespan of Semakau Landfill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The third reason to care about food waste is climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is an issue I have spoken up about repeatedly in this House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that Singapore has committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Reducing food waste is an often-overlooked climate solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Producing food and transporting it takes up valuable resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When we waste food, we also waste the energy and water it takes to produce the food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Noor Hanisah, a Good Samaritan Legislation Review Committee Member and an activist from the Singapore Youth for Climate Action, shared, I quote, “Food waste is one of Singapore’s biggest waste streams.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And we often do not realise that each part of the food journey from production, transportation, handling to wastage have huge carbon footprints that worsen climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Good Samaritan Food Donation Law can reduce this through excess food distribution to the ones in need.” This Bill will also help address a fourth problem which Noor Hanisah spoke about.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am also glad that we have mandated food waste segregation for treatment and reporting this year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we must remember that much of the food wasted is edible food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to recycling food waste, redistributing excess edible food is another solution we must explore, especially when many people in Singapore still go to bed hungry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Food insecurity is when a household does not have access to sufficient, adequate food for a healthy life.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the figures represent a minority of the population, the numbers are still significant and troubling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The study found that food insecurity is associated with serious physical and mental health effects.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We address the issue of food security, we extend the lifespan of the Semakau Landfill, we tackle climate change and we increase the food redistributed to needy families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During our consultations, I heard outrageous stories about the type of perfectly edible food that goes to waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Chickens that are bruised are rejected because they do not meet beauty standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Juicy fruits and crunchy vegetables are dumped because of their imperfect shape or colour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The food that we waste while others go hungry is astounding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government recognised the need to address liability in food donation as early as 2014, nearly 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ms Tan Poh Hong, CEO of what was at the time the Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority of Singapore, said: "A lot of people do not want to donate   in case someone gets food poisoning and sues you.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not saying we are going to have this   law, but we are learning from other countries." In August 2019, the Singapore Environment Council (SEC) published a report which found that the lack of liability protection for donors means that traders, distributors and wholesalers prefer throwing instead of donating food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: SEC noted that a possible solution is introducing policies to safeguard entities from liability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The study found that such a law will address the important concern of liability that businesses face.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government, our NGOs and our youths have all spoken up for a long time for a Good Samaritan Food Donation law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we are finally taking this step forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill is an important step forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a Bill for the people, by the people and for our planet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like the buffet restaurant in my story earlier, many businesses are understandably worried about being liable for someone falling ill from eating the food they donate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses have to worry about potential liability under common law negligence and potential penalties under the Sale of Food Act, the Food Regulations, the Environmental Public Health (Food Hygiene) Regulations and the Penal Code, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Dellen Soh, the Chairman and CEO of Minor Food Singapore and Committee Member of the Restaurant Association of Singapore (RAS) shared, "Many restaurants want to do good.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Restaurants do want to donate excess edible food to reduce food waste and help the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the very risk of liability from donated food has a chilling effect for many restaurants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, food waste may be priced into the cost of business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the concern of legal liability is obviously very significant for restaurants with 80% of those surveyed remaining unsure whether the law will adequately protect businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This underscores what significant chilling effect the risk of liability has on restaurants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through this speech and the debate on this Bill, I hope to clarify how this Bill will protect donors who have done all that they can to ensure the safety and hygiene of donated food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope to allay the very valid concerns and uncertainties restaurants have.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Food charities too have to worry about liability under these laws that I have mentioned.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I want to stress that we should never compromise on food safety and hygiene, whether the food is donated or sold.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, food donors and charities who have done all that they can to ensure that donated food is safe for consumption should not be punished for doing good because of things beyond their control.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After a food donor or charity has donated the food, a recipient may still fall ill from consuming the food if the food is not properly handled or consumed within a safe period by the recipient.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, if a food donor or charity has taken all steps to ensure that the donated food is safe, they should be able to donate food with peace of mind from liability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is what we are proposing to do with the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many other countries have implemented their own food donation laws to address the concerns of liability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These laws have been effective in increasing food donation and still safeguard food hygiene and safety standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The US introduced this law nearly 30 years ago in 1996.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After this law was passed, 7-Eleven announced that the law would allow the company to increase its food donations by as much as 150% over two years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many other jurisdictions have similar laws, including Italy, Alberta in Canada, New South Wales, South Australia and Tasmania in Australia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Marina Bay Sands shared, "Donating surplus food is important to Marina Bay Sands, demonstrated by our long-standing partnerships with Food from the Heart and The Food Bank Singapore, which have allowed us to donate over 51,000 kilogrammes of unserved food to communities in need between 2016 and 2023.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We support the Bill and hope it will encourage other companies to donate food more regularly and reduce food waste." Mr Sebastian Chung, who is the Director of Safety, Health, Environment and Food Hygiene at Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group said, "The implementation of the Good Samaritan Food Donation legislation will help to protect hotels against possible liabilities when re-distributing surplus food responsibly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will encourage hotels to proactively embrace the 3Rs (Reduce, Reuse and Recycle) of food waste management and to support Singapore's vision of becoming a Zero Waste Nation." I have shared why we are proposing a waiver of liability but let me stress again and make clear that a waiver of liability cannot be a shield for those who donate unsafe and unhygienic food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the RAS' survey, all restaurants surveyed indicated that food safety and hygiene was a concern they had with the implementation of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These four conditions strike a balance between encouraging food donation through the waiver of liability and safeguarding food hygiene and safety standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Committee took pains to ensure that the Bill takes a balanced approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The waiver of civil and criminal liability is very carefully scoped and accompanied with the necessary safeguards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I will talk about the scope of persons covered by the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, I will talk about the definition of food donations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, I will talk about the four conditions to be protected from civil and criminal liability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill defines a "food donor" to mean a person who donates food or an entity which donates food in the course of a business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A food donor can be an entity or an individual.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The entity does not need to be a registered charity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill does not differentiate between an individual, a community food rescue group, a religious organisation, a business or a registered food charity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A food donor will cover those who donate food directly to beneficiaries, as well as those who donate food to an intermediary, such as The Food Bank or Food from the Heart, for ultimate distribution to beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the Bill will cover soup kitchens and non-profit organisations that donate food to needy communities, food businesses giving away its surplus canned food products to an aged care establishment for consumption by residents at that establishment, and local restaurants and grocery stores that allow individuals to pick up free food from their outlets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Now that we have discussed the definition of a food donor, let us talk about what constitutes a food donation under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 2 defines "food" to have the same meaning as in the Sale of Food Act 1973.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may include packaged food, like canned food, bottled food or food packed and sealed in a plastic packaging, perishable food, like cakes or bread, cooked food, beverages, fruits and raw vegetables.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 2 also defines "donate" to mean a person giving to another anything for a charitable, benevolent, or philanthropic purpose.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The definition of "donate" also covers a person giving a thing donated by another for a charitable, benevolent or philanthropic purpose.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that the Bill covers both direct and indirect giving, as long as the purpose of the giving is charitable, benevolent or philanthropic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Any person can be considered a recipient of food donations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no requirement that the recipient must be from a certain income group for the Bill to apply.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill will not apply if any money is exchanged for the food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes any fee charged by the donor for providing the food, even if the sum is a nominal sum or is lower than market price.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, clause 3 sets out the purposes of the Bill which are to reduce food waste and to increase availability of food for redistribution to food‑insecure communities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I now move on to the waiver of civil and criminal liability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 4 protects a food donor from civil and criminal liability in respect of any death or personal injury that results from consuming the food donated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The protection applies to all food donors, regardless of whether the food is donated directly to consumers or given to an intermediary, such as a food bank.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It also does not matter whether the intermediary is a charity or a profit‑making social enterprise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is to balance the interest of donors with that of ultimate recipients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These conditions are not intended to be onerous for food donors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, the Committee believes that these conditions will benefit the food donation ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beneficiaries would have confidence that the donated food is safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The safeguards also prevent potential abuse of the waiver.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through our consultations, we arrived at these conditions which are, in fact, best practices that many food donors are already following.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the food donor must inform the recipient of any particular requirements to handle the food to ensure it remains safe to consume.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, the food donor must inform the recipient of any time limit within which the food remains safe and suitable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, the donor must take all reasonable measures to comply with food safety and hygiene requirements up to the point of donation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, being shielded from liability does not take away the Singapore Food Agency's (SFA's) powers to investigate any food safety issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If any food safety issue arises with donated food, SFA can still investigate and take enforcement action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The difference is that food donors only need to show SFA that they have met the four conditions and SFA would not impose any liability on the food donor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Good Samaritan Legislation Review Committee Members, The Food Bank Singapore and Food from the Heart helped to come up with these practical steps that donors can take to fulfil these requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are examples of many different ways that a food donor can fulfil the conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A food donor does not have to do all the practical steps listed here to enjoy liability protections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, these are just suggestions so that everyone can better understand the four conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first requirement is that the food was not unsafe and unsuitable at the time it was donated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A food donor can show that the food was not unsafe and unsuitable by showing, for example, that the food donated had a reasonable period before its expiry date or that cooked food was donated within the four-hour timeframe recommended by SFA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A food donor can also show that it has processes to ensure that the donated food was properly packed and that the packaging was not damaged.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, Food from the Heart has guidelines on packaging of donated bread and the type of bread that it will accept from bakeries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This can be as simple as requiring donated bread to be tied up in plastic bags or not accepting buns with fillings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They also ask that homes and self-collection centres check the bread for mold, pest infestation, bad smells, before distributing to beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second requirement is that the food donor must inform the recipient of any particular requirements to handle the food to ensure it remains safe to consume.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These handling requirements may include proper refrigeration, heating, storage temperatures and packaging requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The food donor can use various means to inform the recipient of handling requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, food donors can ensure that each individual package of donated food has a sticker label informing the recipients of handling requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Food donors can also have a sign with handling requirements at the location where donated food is collected or they can verbally brief recipients on the handling requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They can either have recipients confirm in writing that they were briefed or can also show that recipients were briefed on handling requirements through messages sent to recipients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The third condition is that the food donor informs the recipient of any time limit within which the food remains safe and suitable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similar to the handling requirements, the food donor can use various means to inform the recipient of any time limit for consuming the food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The key is to ensure that the food donor has proper documentation of the information conveyed to recipients on the time limit for consuming food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fourth condition is that the donor took all reasonable measures to comply with food safety and hygiene requirements up to the point of donation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One key document here is the SFA Guidelines for Social Service Agencies and Community Groups Involved in Food Preparation and Distribution Activities for Charitable Causes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That was a mouthful and is probably the longest name for any guideline.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, the donor can have a standard operating procedure (SOP) for its food donation operations and training for its volunteers which complies with food safety and hygiene requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As an example, again, Food from the Heart requires its donors to fulfil its SOPs for its Bread Run.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Volunteers are also required to comply with the SOPs, including that bread must be collected and redistributed on the same day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All four conditions must be proven before protection can apply.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I should stress that the defendant seeking protection has the burden of proof.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proposal was surveyed in a public consultation and there was some support for accreditation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Committee also received feedback from smaller food charities and food rescue groups that accreditation will make donation activities more onerous.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We did not want the Bill to have the unintended consequence of dissuading food donations by imposing conditions that are too difficult to achieve.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even then, the Committee recognises that food donors could use some help to incorporate the proof of meeting these conditions into their operations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE), SFA and the Ministry of Social and Family Development will continue to engage the industry and food charities and provide this support that is very much needed on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first scenario is where food is exchanged between individuals as part of a personal relationship.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, the Bill would not apply to giving food to friends or snacks in the office pantry bought for colleagues even though no money is exchanged.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second scenario is where food is provided together with accommodation to an individual in a private residence in exchange for services or labour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that employers would not receive a waiver for food provided to their domestic helpers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am grateful to Ms Elyssa Chua from Breadtalk; Ms Adalia Tan from DBS Bank; Mr Robin Lee from Food from the Heart; Mr Tan Hang Chong from Foodscape Collective; Ms Soh Li Sar from NTUC Fairprice; Mr Dellen Soh from the Restaurant Association of Singapore and Minor Food Group Singapore; Mr Sebastian Chung from the Singapore Hotel Association and Mandarin Oriental Singapore; Ms Noor Hanisah from the Singapore Youth for Climate Action; Mr Nicholas Ng from The Food Bank Singapore; Ms Jeanne Ng from The Fullerton Hotels and Resorts; Mr Jesher Loi from Ya Kun International; grassroots leaders Ms Chua Wei-Shan and Mr Wong Jin Feng; and my fellow Members of Parliament, Ms Poh Li San, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Edward Chia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He was invited to be a part of the Good Samaritan Legislation Review Committee but could not make it due to his health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nizar was an inspiration to many for his work in providing food to the needy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure he would be very proud to see what we have accomplished today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: His legacy of giving to others will continue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe that he first flagged food waste as an issue back in 2018 before following up with a suggestion for a Good Samaritan Act in 2020.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Bill today is a culmination of his efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I should also disclose, at the outset, that there are currently various food rescue and distribution programmes in operation across Sengkang Group Representation Constituency (GRC), the constituency that I serve, and that I and my fellow Sengkang Members of Parliament have, at various times in the past, participated in these community-led initiatives while also offering our support to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is also the case for several other Workers' Party divisions in Hougang and Aljunied GRCs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The four stipulations, outlined in clause 4 of the Bill, delineate these conditions while ensuring consistency with existing laws.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notably, however, the observed duration is a guideline and, as far as I am aware, not mandated by law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This strikes me as fair since we do not wish to excessively police folks who may decide to tapao leftovers, nor would a blanket requirement cater for the wide variation in windows for safe consumption of different types of food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, I would be far more comfortable stuffing my face with a day-old cupcake, for instance, than I would with a day-old plate of laksa.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, how would the fact that these existing guidelines not crossing the threshold of the law alter the stipulation in Part D?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would a potential donor be able to pass along leftover food that had been in a buffet line for four and a half hours to the youth hostel next door, for example, under this Bill?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that Part C does insist on informing recipients of the timeline for safe consumption, but does this also imply that donating food that exceeds this duration is permissible so long as this step is undertaken?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would it perhaps be safer, for the case of cooked food, that a "donated food" label be affixed?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This approach aligns with the US Department of Agriculture's definition of "qualifying food" under the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, I would suggest that line 19 on page 5 consider the inclusion of this term so that it would read "A food donor who donates any food in good faith shall not, in fact, be liable" and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, on each of those occasions, the then-Ministers of Law explained that such legislation was unnecessary since both civil and criminal liability would generally be waived for those acting in good faith and it was stated explicitly that "our current laws strike the correct balance".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Granted, the context of those Good Samaritan discussions was distinct and applicable more to the provision of on-site physical or medical assistance to those in need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, such laws in many other jurisdictions actually compel aid, whereas the Bill in question today is essentially voluntary in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, I believe it is fair to ask why this particular Good Samaritan law, which waives liability in a voluntary context, is deemed necessary while an analogous law that would do the same for involuntary harm is not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, I think it is useful for us to put ourselves in the mindset of those rendering aid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would their knowledge of the potential for liability inhibit their choice to render succour even if the law would not explicitly hold them to account?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would it be better to have the waiver made explicit, as it is in this present Bill, albeit in a different context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, MSE can support the development of, potentially, an online database of potential food donors and recipients to promote scaling up at the national level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could then become a one-stop shop which matches those in the F&B industry with those with a desire to contribute back to the community and social welfare groups, such as food banks or grassroots organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will relieve these groups from the need to maintain their own independent network of suppliers and distributors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will also help imbalances of access where certain more-connected groups are able to leverage their establishment connections to acquire a higher volume of donations but may be left with perhaps an embarrassment of riches even as other groups face shortages.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Consistent with the thrust of the present Bill, the site can also prominently post reminders, perhaps even explicitly require donors to declare that the four stipulations of clause 4 of this Bill are being adhered to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, I believe that the pervasiveness of residents participating in food rescue programmes hints at the squeezed middle class in our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While some of these participating households are undoubtedly doing so out of an abundance of thrift or a desire to promote sustainable living, many that I have spoken to do so because the regular channels of support are unavailable to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By way of conclusion, I wish to thank the many donors, coordinators and food banks that have already stepped forward to support food sustainability programmes across the nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They have done so despite the potential liability exposure that they could have faced prior to this piece of legislation and this speaks to both their commitment as well as courage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And for all the so-called "Food Rescue Uncles and Aunties" who have been tirelessly working to distribute food to those in need, week after week, including in our town of Sengkang, thank you.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, recipients are protected as there are clear specifications to ensure that the food donated meet hygiene requirements and delivery timeframes for food safety.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill will also go a long way to cut down on the unfortunately huge amounts of food waste in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many other countries had already enacted similar legislation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Canada has similar laws with slight differences in each province.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Australia, the Civil Liability Amendment (Food Donations) Act 2005 offers similar protections too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Five years ago, Japan introduced the Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction to reduce food waste and support food banks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is a crying shame that much of perfectly safe and edible food are thrown away every day while the most vulnerable segments of our society face food insecurity.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This new legislation will help suppliers and sellers overcome their concerns about liabilities and donate to those in need.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Companies involved in food donation can enhance their reputation and image.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Based on the information and food data available, there is more than enough food to feed our needy regularly and nutritiously.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition to reducing food waste, food donation will reduce our environmental impact and footprint associated with the wastage.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to raise my concerns to the relevant Government departments.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the relevant Ministry ensure that staff and volunteers receive regular training on food safety practices?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will there be requirements to prove traceability of the donated items, such as the maintenance of records, to ensure accountability in case issues arise?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry conduct audits or regular inspections to check on the food quality and safety standards?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will donors be encouraged or be required to have liability insurance as an extra layer of protection?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will SFA foster partnerships between donors and reputable charities to ensure the proper distribution and use of donated food, avoid duplicate deliveries and prevent abuse of donations, such as reselling?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will public accountability measures be implemented, such as the collection and publication of donation data and impact reports?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): By implementing these strategies, I am confident that Singapore can optimise the benefits of the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill, while mitigating the risks and preventing potential abuse of the system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill that we are debating today helps to promote more acts of kindness in our society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a tremendous amount of waste, which is even more regrettable because we import more than 90% of our food.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party (PSP) hopes that the enactment of this Bill will encourage more F&B premises, food producers and retailers to be kind and donate excess food instead of throwing it away.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this Bill, these donors will be shielded from liability from deaths or health issues from the consumption of cooked food, provided that four conditions are met.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that these conditions, which include ensuring that the food must not be unsafe at the time it was donated and the food donor must inform the food recipient of the handling requirements, are reasonable and should not pose an excessive impediment to food donors.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even though we live in an era of great material abundance and our country has achieved great economic progress, there are still some amongst us who are struggling to even put food on the table.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a nation, we can and should do more to help this group of vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will also have a positive impact on the environment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Food waste is one of our biggest waste streams, accounting for about 11% of the waste generated in Singapore in 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any reduction in food waste will go towards extending the lifespan of Semakau Landfill.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, would-be food donors may face logistical challenges in transporting their excess food to food distribution centres or charities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can also consider providing tax incentives to transport or platform companies to assist in this effort by providing food pickup and delivery services for larger F&B enterprises.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, PSP supports the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In February this year, I spoke about the importance of being kind, which would go a long way towards improving our collective mental health.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill that we are debating today, will exempt businesses or individuals donating food from liability.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This helps promote more acts of kindness in our society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is said that food is of utmost importance to people.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In prosperous Singapore, approximately one in 10 households lack sufficient access to food.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, every day, we throw away more than two million kilogrammes of food.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of these discarded food items are still safe for consumption.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they can be redistributed to food-insecure households, it would benefit numerous families.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides passing this Bill, the Government can consider implementing tax reliefs to businesses to encourage them to donate excess food.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, some food donors may face logistical challenges in transporting food.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can also consider providing tax incentives to transport or platform companies to assist by providing delivery services and deliver the donated food to charities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In doing so, we can also reduce the food waste in Singapore, contributing to environmental conservation efforts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that after this Bill is passed, more companies and individuals will step up and generously donate excess food to help the needy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): Sir, I hope that after this Bill is passed, more companies and individuals will step up and generously donate the excess food after their catering events or unsold food at the end of the day to the needy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There will always be someone out there who will appreciate having that food on the table.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us reduce food waste and build a kinder Singapore together.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had made a few observations regarding the Bill and statements made by various Ministers for Law in response to questions.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And I was one of those, at that time, Senior Minister of State for Law, who had addressed a question on the point of Good Samaritan Bills.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I believe Assoc Prof Lim asked why this particular Good Samaritan law is deemed necessary, when an analogous law that would do the same for involuntary harm by a helpful bystander would not.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And actually, the question, if you had listened to his speech, was actually answered by Assoc Prof Lim himself.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: He had said this, and I quote, "Granted, the context of those Good Samaritan discussions was distinct and applicable more to the provision of on-site physical or medical assistance to those in need.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Importantly, such laws in many other jurisdictions compel aid, whereas the Bill in question is essentially voluntary in nature." And that is exactly right.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In short, the context of the previous Parliamentary Questions (PQs) and the replies to them is different.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The previous PQs referred to Good Samaritan laws in the context of rendering medical or emergency assistance to people who are ill or injured.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, in his reply, Prof Jayakumar explained that Good Samaritan laws adopted in other countries broadly take two forms.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, to reduce bystanders' hesitation to render assistance because of significant liability concerns.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In these jurisdictions, there are laws granting persons who offer aid in emergency situations, certain protections from legal liability.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And second, to impose a positive legal requirement on people to assist others in distress, unless they will put themselves in danger.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: On the first point, that is, to overcome bystanders' hesitation, the various Ministers for Law explained in their replies that, in Singapore, we have not encountered reluctance on the part of our citizens to step forward to help in those emergency situations.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And on the second point, Prof Jayakumar said that helpful bystanders do not face any major liability concerns in Singapore.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For civil liability, a person who offers assistance need only comply with what is expected of a person of his or her skills or experience, so an untrained person would not be held to the standard of a doctor, for example.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As for criminal liability, that is generally premised on an intent to cause harm or injury.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A person who has acted reasonably and in good faith is unlikely to be held criminally liable.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The context of the current Good Samaritan Bill is different.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: And this is different from the emergency scenarios addressed by the Ministers for Law, where they have not encountered reluctance to step forward and there are no major liability concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I could clarify, since the Minister did suggest that she had spoken about this Good Samaritan law elsewhere before, do all other jurisdictions compel the rendering of aid?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Are there some Good Samaritan laws that simply waive liability?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I ask this because in that case, then analogous to this law, the idea of providing that peace of mind to bystanders that may choose to render aid, I think, would nevertheless still be helpful.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I had actually addressed that earlier, because he asked whether all jurisdictions compel bystanders to provide aid.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And as I had explained, which was also explained by Prof Jayakumar, there are two forms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in other words, it is because people are reluctant to step forward and help.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And in some other jurisdictions, they take a more aggressive approach and they say you must help.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But of course, having said you must help, then the corollary is you also provide the waiver of liability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in short, there is no one-size-fits-all, you have a law where there is a need or you assess that you want to do it for a particular reason.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this case, this Bill is a Private Member's Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The need, as I understand it, is Mr Louis Ng feels that people are hesitant to donate because they are concerned about liability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if you are a doctor, you are held to a higher standard.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you are just an ordinary person helping out, you are held to that standard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just one note and that is, I do not think we can actually know if it is true that someone who is hesitant has not actually hesitated to step up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Because we do not observe all those individuals that have stepped up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I am wondering if the Minister would agree with me that, indeed, we will never know the counterfactual to the situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had missed reports in the newspapers from the last few days.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I was present at Home Team's National Day Observance Ceremony at the Home Team Academy and there were dozens of members of the public who had voluntarily stepped forward in emergency situations to help others.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, perhaps, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, would like to look at those news reports and see for himself.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Indranee, would you like to respond as well?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am sorry, Sir, because I was listening to Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean and I had forgotten Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's question, would the Member like to repeat it?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The question is whether, it is not so much whether we observe that some people are indeed stepping forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am certain that is the case and we have news reports that say this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is fundamentally unobservable as a counterfactual and, that is why, I asked whether the Minister would agree that we would not know the full extent to which individuals have not stepped forward.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If all of us encourage members of the public to do so and tell them not to be afraid, I am sure they would do so and more of them would do more and not be hesitant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean's point is perfectly well taken, which is that it is good to encourage people to step up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While this Bill has noble intentions, I have several clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, while the Bill seeks to address liability concerns, we must also consider the practical aspects of encouraging greater participation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The intent alone, while admirable, may not be sufficient to shift behaviour on a larger scale.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What specific incentives or support mechanisms are being considered to motivate eateries or bakeries to donate their surplus food?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Although liability protection is a step forward, it is essentially removing a barrier; we must now provide and encourage people to be more active.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To this end, I urge the Government to consider tangible incentives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Subsidies for logistical costs associated with donated food, particularly for smaller businesses, could also boost participation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, public recognition programmes, perhaps, a "Food Rescue Champion" award, could incentivise businesses through positive reinforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By incorporating such proactive measures, we can transform this Bill from a shield against liability, into a sword actively combating food waste.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, clear and consistent communication is paramount to ensure clarity and safety for recipients.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A visible and clear "consume by" label could minimise the risk of foodborne illnesses arising from miscommunication or forgetfulness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such labels would serve as a visual vivid reminder, even after verbal communication has taken place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could empower recipients to make informed decisions about food consumption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can also provide an additional layer of protection for well-intended donors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would also foster greater trust and transparency within the food donation ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must consider the feasibility of implementing such labelling requirements, particularly for smaller businesses involved in food.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A balanced approach, perhaps, with exemptions or tailored guidelines for different types of food donations, may be necessary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, greater clarity is needed on the Bill’s stance on community fridges and food rescue initiatives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While we strive to ensure the safety and suitability of donated food, we must also recognise the valuable contributions of initiatives operating at the community level.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These initiatives often involve collecting and redistributing food that might be aesthetically imperfect or nearing its "best by" date.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Explicit inclusion would provide these groups with much-needed legal assurance and encourage their growth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This allows them to expand their reach and impact on minimising food waste in addition to supporting vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must not overlook the critical issue of food allergies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These can present significant, even life-threatening risks, if not managed carefully.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I seek clarification on how this Bill addresses the potential for allergic reactions, particularly, in situations where donors may not be fully aware of the allergen content in the food they are donating.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Among food-insecure groups, those with allergies already face an uphill battle in balancing their dietary needs with financial constraints.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While some might suggest that individuals with allergies could simply avoid donated food with unclear labelling, this ignores a critical aspect of food insecurity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By denying themselves access to potentially safe and nutritious food due to a lack of information, individuals with allergies are deprived of economical choices that could significantly ease their burdens.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Collaboration with health authorities to develop a standardised allergen labelling system, perhaps drawing from existing regulations requiring businesses to declare known food allergens on their food labels, would be invaluable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be done for common allergies, like seafood, nuts or gluten, if they are known to be present in the donated food.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, greater efforts could be made to educate food donors on best practices for minimising allergen consumption risks, such as avoiding cross-contamination and providing accurate ingredient information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Speaker, Sir, as a multicultural society, we must respect and accommodate the diverse dietary needs of our population, especially those with specific religious or cultural requirements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, Muslims are required to consume Halal food and Hindus and many Buddhists abstain from consuming beef.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I urge the Government to outline guidelines for donors to follow, preventing unintentional non-compliance with these various dietary standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear and accurate labelling of ingredients, particularly when it comes to potentially "sensitive" ingredients like beef or pork products, is paramount in empowering recipients to make informed choices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Resources should also be made available on proper handling and labelling, to ensure that food intended for halal consumption remains untainted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But in cases where this is not practical or where such oversights occur despite best efforts, does the Bill offer legal protection for donors who unintentionally provide food that does not align with a recipient's religious dietary needs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Addressing this aspect thoughtfully will not only demonstrate our commitment to inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can also instil greater confidence in the food donation system, encouraging wider participation from both donors and recipients.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sixth, Mr Speaker, Sir, it is equally critical that we ensure faithful compliance to food safety and hygiene.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The success of this initiative hinges on maintaining public trust in the safety and quality of donated food.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I seek clarification on how the Bill will ensure that food donors are well-informed and fully compliant with existing food safety and hygiene laws.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These situations, often involving catering or bulk cooking, can increase the likelihood of issues, such as undercooking, improper storage and prolonged exposure to hot weather, a concern further amplified by Singapore's rising temperatures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is also precisely such events, where large volumes of food might otherwise go to waste, that could benefit most from the food donation framework established by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, we must be particularly vigilant in mitigating the risks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to consider incorporating targeted guidelines and training for donors handling large quantities of food, emphasising best practices for safe storage and transportation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These programmes could be developed in collaboration with relevant agencies, like SFA, providing donors with the knowledge and skills to handle food safely throughout the donation process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, raising awareness among recipients about the importance of thoroughly reheating donated food, where possible, before consumption, could further minimise the risk of foodborne illnesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, I seek clarifications on the Bill's broader implications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill has the potential to be more than just a legal framework.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can be a catalyst for positive change in how we, as a nation, approach food waste and food security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To fully realise this potential, I believe it is vital that the Ministry provides us with a broader perspective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What are the long-term goals and strategic vision underlining this Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A clear understanding of the Bill's intended impact beyond the immediate legal implications would be invaluable to all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will enable us to identify potential synergies, areas for future refinement and opportunities for collaborative action.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can empower businesses, organisations and individuals to play a meaningful role in building a more sustainable and food-secure future for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our Food Rescue programme, run entirely by volunteers, sees about 60 dedicated individuals, many of them youths from nearby schools, including Presbyterian High, Nanyang Polytechnic, the Institute of Technical Education Central and so on, coming together every fortnight to volunteer their time in the name of sustainability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They help to collect imperfect or expiring food from wholesale centres and shops that would have otherwise gone to waste.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They sort out and throw away parts that cannot be eaten and redistribute the good and edible portions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have about 200 regular residents who participate in this programme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Both our Prime Minister and Senior Minister Lee have witnessed how our Food Rescue Programme works during their visits to Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, as much as we strive for careful sorting and quality control, there are always inherent risks associated with redistributing food that are deemed commercially unsellable or nearing its expiry date, particularly when problematic food products are unintentionally overlooked during the sorting process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill would play a vital role in addressing these concerns, providing legal clarity and peace of mind for those involved in such initiatives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the Bill is a significant step in the right direction, I believe that addressing the points and questions that I have raised today will further strengthen its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, to truly shift behavior on a larger scale, we should go beyond merely removing legal barriers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Offering tangible incentives, such as tax benefits, logistical support and public recognition, could significantly motivate more eateries and bakeries to participate in food donation efforts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear labelling is another important aspect that should be mandated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Providing these groups with legal assurance would encourage their growth and amplify their impact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, this Bill must address the issue of food allergies, which pose significant risks if not properly managed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clear guidelines for allergen labelling are essential to protect those with food allergies, ensuring that they have safe access to donated food.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It aligns perfectly with the spirit of Forward Singapore, where sustainability is a key pillar.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By addressing these key areas and working collaboratively with all stakeholders, we can build a more sustainable and compassionate society in Singapore.
