speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For the Bill to improve food security for those in need, steps must be taken to ensure that surplus food can be channelled safely and efficiently in sustainable and long-lasting arrangements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to suggest three measures for the Review Committee and the Government to consider alongside Bill implementation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would incentivise businesses to formalise food donation activities which would in turn stabilise food aid supply in Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: There is precedent implementation of such initiative in Colombia.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I would suggest a closer study of this initiative as there could be valuable learning for Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, if well implemented, the Bill would elevate the extent and scale of food rescue and redistribution.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would mean that food rescue organisations would hope for more resources and support to enhance cold chains, to cater for adequate storage facilities and to continually train their staff and volunteers to know how to keep different types of food safe for consumption.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, the well-being of recipients is priority and I hope that the Bill can open doors for more of such help to flow.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, food rescue and redistribution efforts must be paired with public-private schemes and support that provide lower-income families with dignified, sustained and adequate access to nutritious food.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Lien Centre for Social Innovation released its Hunger Report in 2020.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The report brought to the fore the stigma surrounding food support.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The report shared that food-insecure individuals more often experienced negative emotions of sadness, stress and embarrassment that might result in them shying away from help to meet food needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because dining out at hawker centres and coffee shops is a mainstay for many Singaporeans, a lower-income family that can partake in affordable hawker meals alongside others in the community could feel more assured and secured in meeting their food needs and less burdened by negative emotions.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This matters because enhanced welfare for vulnerable families should not be at the expense of economic survival of hawkers, many of whom are self-employed and are working hard to make a living.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In summary, this Bill is a step towards building a kinder society.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It shines a light on how some businesses and individuals have helped and how more businesses and individuals can now come forward to help to channel safe, surplus food to households struggling to meet food needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: By strengthening empathy and connections among the broader public, the Bill is a game-changer that can help to dismantle the social stigma surrounding food support while giving food-insecure families the confidence to benefit from food support that is dignified, sustained, adequate and enriching.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Food rescue organisations, despite their best efforts, may not be able to thoroughly inspect every donated item.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Therefore, it is crucial to clarify whether the Bill will also protect these intermediary groups and who would be held liable if unsafe food is distributed.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, some food rescue social enterprises may ask for donations or nominal fees to support sustainability efforts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is important to determine if the Bill will cover these groups and establish requirements for their inclusion.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Moving on to points for consideration, it is essential to complement the implementation of the Bill with public education.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This broadens the acceptance of rescued foods and should inform individuals on the different date labels, such as the distinction between "expiry," "best before" and "use by" dates.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Understanding the difference between safety-based versus quality-based date labels is crucial to reducing household food waste.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Additionally, educating consumers on what shelf-stable items are is equally vital, especially since overseas manufacturers may not use date labelling terms accurately.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Items, such as soy sauce, uncooked rice or salt, can be kept almost indefinitely when properly stored, further supporting this effort.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Rescued food should be embraced by everyone, not just those in need.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While it is crucial to prioritise the needy in distributing donated food, it is equally important for the entire society to cultivate a mindset focused on reducing food waste for meaningful and collective effective efforts in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While liability protection such as the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill removes barriers to food donation, tax incentives directly encourage food donation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Food donors need to invest time and resources in packing, storing and especially in transporting surplus food.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These food items would otherwise be discarded, often at no cost to them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Tax incentives can help offset these expenses for them.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In Japan and Australia, companies that adopt innovative waste reduction methods, such as tech-enabled inventory management, receive substantial government support and recognition.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Voluntary commitments by organisations across the food system, such as those seen in Australia and the United Kingdom (UK), with initiatives like the Courtauld Commitment, have created industry-wide movements to reduce food waste.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These efforts are also strongly supported by the respective governments.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By defining liability and expanding protection to social enterprises and food rescue organisations, we enhance its impact across the broader community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Addressing food waste requires a collective effort from the entire nation and demands a widespread societal transformation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Beyond legislation, it is essential to implement programmes that educate consumers while requiring businesses to take proactive steps in reducing food wastage.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am confident that together, we can establish a more sustainable and responsible food system in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I would also commend him on the brevity and general simplicity of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In introducing this Bill, Mr Ng mentioned it had been a four-year journey.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Food wastage cannot continue to increase without responsible response at both national and international levels.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many initiatives continue in this attempt to curb food wastage.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We must do our part in Singapore to reduce food wastage across all the areas, within our ability to do so.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Most of us in Singapore are blessed with the ability to afford all our meals.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We are, however, aware that there are communities in our midst facing challenges to place food on the table, each meal, for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: If each household took action to distribute some or most of this, Mr Louis Ng will see the tangible results of reducing unnecessary food waste and, concurrently, making food available for the food-insecure communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I accept that this may be too simplistic and general.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Though efforts in this direction can result in many, many more good Samaritans stepping forward across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The parable of the Good Samaritan illustrated that we can and should show love for everyone beyond just family and friends.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The food and beverage (F&B) industry continues to face high operating costs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, cost of food, whether raw or prepared, is often carefully controlled.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Most operators will control inventory to minimise spoilage from overstocking perishable items.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are constant efforts to keep improving operational efficiencies and managing the bottom line.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Controlling food wastage at source is primary in a sustainable F&B business.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Most commercial F&B operators require licensing and follow strict compliance requirements toward food safety and hygiene.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Cooked food is to be consumed within stipulated time limits and consumers are provided with this information.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Owing to the health and safety regulations and also the cost controls by F&B operators, there would seem to be limited amounts of prepared or cooked food suitable for donation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some foods, such as breads and pastries that have longer shelf life, may remain safe for consumption, though the quality may be affected after a period of time.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, this does not suggest that the F&B industry cannot still be Good Samaritans.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I would encourage the F&B industry, wholesalers and retailers of food in all forms, to be generous and work with groups, including the hon Member, to make available food to meet the basic needs of food-insecure sectors of our communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many F&B operators donated generously during COVID-19 and this spirit of generosity can find new avenues as we strive toward a more caring society, caring for each other and also caring for the environment.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Moving to the other sectors of food, may I suggest that wholesalers and retailers review the timelines set on donating food reaching expiry dates?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It is, of course, clear that every business needs to stay profitable and viable.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, for those that continue to do well, perhaps donating dry goods with a longer shelf life can achieve the dual objectives of reduced wastage and more food for those who can benefit from such donations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Louis Ng did a great deal of research and consultation in the four years and has reached some level of confidence that by absolving donors of liability there would be more food available for donation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In his opening remarks, Mr Louis Ng mentioned that with the removal of liability, some hotels and restaurants would be prepared to step forward and donate food.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I initially struggled with the exemption of liability on some basic principles.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The intended beneficiaries are fellow human beings who must retain their dignity and basic rights.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In all likelihood, they would be vulnerable and, therefore, may need guidance.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, if they do get ill from consuming donated food, they would have the added struggle of medical costs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It remained unclear to me what possible circumstances could contribute to illness if the food donated was safe and healthy at the point of donation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Could Mr Louis Ng provide us some examples the Bill intends to address this?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Through this Bill, Mr Ng has continued to advocate for the need to being responsible in the area of food wastage and highlighting the existing needs of fellow citizens and residents who do not have access to three meals a day.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We must continue to work on both these areas.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Successful implementation, looking ahead, could, therefore, bring us to this scenario where: firstly, efforts to reduce food wastage bring good results; secondly, food will still find its way to the food-insecure as part of the reduction in food wastage; thirdly, there may, however, be less food available for donation from the many sources as food wastage reduces.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, hopefully, when we get to that stage, there will be a sizeable reduction in those in our community who continue to be food-insecure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is always a shame to waste food and in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The same article suggested at least half of this is in the form of bread, rice and noodles.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill aims to alleviate some of this food wastage.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of these are the same matters that the authorities would look into even today if there is a complaint.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The main difference is this legislation sets out a positive list of requirements, which if met, would mean the food donors do not have to worry about liability from their food being eaten by recipients.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are many organisations and people that currently collect and redistribute food from potential donors to recipients.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill aims to support the work of these organisations and groups by making their legal responsibilities clear and easy to comply with.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of the ways to reduce this wastage and contribute to food sustainability is to get suppliers and stores to donate their buffer stocks and surpluses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As storage space is costly, many companies have found it easier to just throw away and dispose of the food.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I strongly urge the Government to do more to educate and incentivise them to donate these precious foods.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This would require some effort and coordination and, hence, I appeal to the Government to provide the necessary administrative and infrastructural support to help them get started on this journey of donation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government, food suppliers and stores, voluntary welfare organisations and volunteers, need to work together to develop an efficient and safe logistical supply chain to effectively channel such food donations to charities and beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I hope that the Government will provide more information to suppliers and commercial entities about the benefits of food donation and implement measures to motivate them to donate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the donation process requires them to provide manpower and other resources and do coordination work, I therefore request the Government to provide the necessary administrative and infrastructure support to help them start on their donation journey.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government, food suppliers and shops, voluntary welfare organisations and volunteers need to work together to develop efficient and safe logistics supply chains to effectively channel these food donations to charities and beneficiaries. : In some countries, such as Spain, businesses could face fines of up to €60,000 if they fail to reduce the amount of food they throw away.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Bill does not propose such a punitive measure, but waiving the liability alone may not be enough to move some suppliers and sellers to donate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill excludes situations of gross negligence, given the requirement that the food donors will still need to comply with all prevailing laws on food safety and food hygiene.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill is also well-crafted in spelling out the responsibilities and duties of each party at every stage of the donation process, while ensuring food safety and hygiene, protecting the recipients.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill presents us with the opportunity to make a meaningful impact, particularly in the realm of community support and philanthropy, to encourage food rescue and food donation without the risk of criminal and civil liability for donors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Allow me to speak in Malay. :   One major aspect that is addressed by this Bill is to facilitate the processes for food contribution and donation, especially during events and important dates such as the month of Ramadan, the Prophet Muhammad's birthday and the Islamic New Year, when many generous donors will donate food for the congregants in the mosques and our community in general.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our mosques, madrasahs and Muslim welfare bodies currently play an essential role, such as preparing dishes for the breaking of fast and pre-dawn meals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many generous Singaporeans are also keen to donate in kind or spend their time cooking for the needy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One inspiring example comes from the Al Firdaus Mosque located in the Keat Hong area.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This mosque has consistently and tirelessly provided and served pre-dawn meals or meals for the breaking of fast for thousands of foreign workers living in the dormitory at Lim Chu Kang, which is near the mosque.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During each Ramadan too, the M3 network in Chua Chu Kang collaborates with the mosque to mobilise the manpower to distribute porridge that was donated by the public regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have visited the mosques in Chua Chu Kang and all of them welcomed this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Previously, mosques that receive food donations would require donors to fill in their details in a form and require them to sign an indemnity form, so that the mosque and volunteers will be released from any claims for damages should anyone fall ill after eating the donated food.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We will also hope to encourage the habits of food savings. : Speaker, in Keat Hong Chua Chu Kang, we receive many generous donations and contributions of food by kind-hearted individuals who want to give back to society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These come from individuals and also food rescue from the nearby farms in Keat Hong.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of them take time to cook each month, specially for this.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Take, for example, Mr Ong, a hawker from Teck Whye market who uses his time off to cook vegetarian bee hoon, which we distribute to residents monthly.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr and Mrs Song, hawkers from Boon Lay, who contribute packets of chicken rice during our People's Action Party (PAP) branch’s free monthly haircut sessions for seniors in Keat Hong.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These efforts have been ongoing in the town for years.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They do this out of the kindness of their hearts but they face the potential risk of liability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is time for us to repay their kindness.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While we welcome this Bill with open arms, it is essential to recognise that it is not a cure-all solution.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One notable inclusion in the Bill is the exclusion of criminal liability, allowing Good Samaritans to step forward and organisations to do more for the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, prudent parties may still wish to take certain precautions, such as obtaining waivers or disclaimers of liability from consumers, seeking indemnity from donors, conducting due diligence on donors where possible and providing training to volunteers and raising awareness among beneficiaries regarding the donated food.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is crucial to strike a balance between responsibility and philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, section 2C of the Sale of Food Act's definition of unsafe food, which definition is imported in this Bill, uses the phrase "cause illness or injury or other physical harm to a person".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This clarity is vital to prevent any ambiguity or disputes in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Based on the current definition used in the Bill, any illness caused by the consumption of the donated food may not be caught under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Back in 2017, in my voluntary role with the self-help group AMP Singapore, we collaborated with Free Food For All to distribute over 9,000 meals to under-privileged households.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It was a record number at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Free Food For All’s founder, the late Mr Nizar Shariff, was a Singaporean of the Year finalist and a winner of the President’s Volunteerism and Philanthropy Awards.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that this Bill represents a significant step forward for us to create more such individuals in our society in fostering a more caring and supportive community, where individuals and organisations can come together to make a positive impact without fear of criminal or civil liability from the donated food.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us embrace this opportunity to extend a helping hand to those in need and create a stronger, more compassionate society for all.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill is the culmination of the close collaboration and consultations with various stakeholders for an important social cause.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For this, I am grateful for having been able to work with my Parliamentary colleagues, Mr Louis Ng, Ms Poh Li San and Mr Edward Chia, alongside our PAP activists as well as industry players, social enterprises, public agencies and the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The passage of this Bill is a milestone but not the end of our journey.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We will continue to engage with the relevant stakeholders and community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There will always be room for further improvements.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The amount was 813,000 tonnes in 2022, and 817,000 tonnes in 2021.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Against this backdrop, and paradoxically, food insecurity remains a live issue.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through our consultations, we learnt that a key concern of our current and prospective food donors is liability, both civil and criminal.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As shared by my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Louis Ng, in his opening speech, there are many donors and potential donors out there who would like to contribute but are understandably concerned about incurring liability, despite taking every precaution and doing their utmost best.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Woodgrove, I am grateful to have many community partners and residents who are supportive of our call to embrace green sustainable living, reduce food waste and do good "For the Community, From the Community".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Several green sustainable events in Woodgrove, both large and small scale, have been held through the years, providing opportunities for residents and community partners, such as schools, to contribute ideas and take part in supporting our nation’s SG Green Plan goals.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Events, such as our Woodgrove's World Environment Day, which is held on an annual basis for our community, would regularly see strong support by our community gardeners, donating their fruits and vegetables that were grown in over 100 plots of community gardens across Woodgrove.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In July 2023, Woodgrove set up our weekly community pantry located at the heart of Woodgrove, where residents are welcomed to help themselves with food rations and daily essential items which were donated by community partners, such as temples, as well as residents who have requested to remain anonymous but chose to do good for our community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am heartened that during a National Day block party in Woodgrove held over a recent weekend, we announced a Woodgrove-FairPrice Group collaboration, under which the FairPrice Group, being Singapore’s largest retailer and one of the working committee members of this Bill, will be on board as another enthusiastic community partner to support our expansion of the community pantry initiative to benefit a larger community in Woodgrove through its Community Fridge Restock Initiative, which aimed at providing blemished but edible fruits and vegetables to families and individuals in need across Singapore for free.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are just some examples of the many good work we have heard that are in progress in the community, which many are looking to operationalise and even expand under and upon the passage of this Bill, for our residents’ and the wider public’s benefit.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the same time, I also hope that the Singapore Food Agency would continue to guide us in this important mission, such as coming up with clear and specific food safety standards and best practices for the purposes of this Bill that will be implemented by all food donors and understood by all of the donees as well.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One particular area would be the public education on the significance and difference between "best by" and "expiry" dates used, like what my Parliamentary colleague, Miss Rachel Ong, has shared earlier.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would these categories of food be, therefore, acceptable and safe for consumption?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   The purpose of this Bill is set out at clause 3, which is to reduce food waste and increase the availability of food for redistribution to food-insecure communities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Perhaps collaterally, this Bill would also hopefully bolster Singapore’s "30 by 30" food security goal.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With less wastage, the need for increased production could be ameliorated.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Recently, there has been a spate of mass food poisoning cases which reminded us the importance of complying with food safety laws when handling food.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As members of the public, either as donors or beneficiaries, we must not take it lightly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope the relevant authorities such as SFA to continue working with community partners to increase public awareness of food safety.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This Bill will help to cut down on food wastage while ensuring food safety and hygiene for recipients.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The liability waiver will go a long way to empower all stakeholders, from the suppliers to donors and volunteers, to save and distribute edible food with peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope all stakeholders can do their part to anticipate demand more precisely and reduce potential wastage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the face of increasing challenges for food production and transportation, due to international conflicts and extreme weather, unpredictable conditions, food prices are expected to keep going up.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving forward, we will have less room for waste.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the greatest concerns we all share is our hot and humid weather condition.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other products, such as bread and fruit, mould within days.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We require a robust cold chain logistics network to support donors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The unpredictable amounts of donated food from different sources pose a challenge for storage and distribution by voluntary welfare organisations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider supporting interested donors to advise and assist them on food storage and transportation?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Suppliers and stores, together with the Government, should also clarify food expiry labels, such as "best before", "use by", "expiry", for the benefit of consumers and donation recipients.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is an important step to reduce the amount of food discarded prematurely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Compared to other countries with similar legislation, such as the US, I would say that our proposed conditions are on par with these other countries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with the proposals in the Bill, such as for the food to meet the Sale of Food Act, that the food must not have been "unsafe" and "unsuitable" for consumption when it leaves the possession or control of the food donor, and that the recipients be informed of handling requirements and time limit for consumption.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the EU, the labels on the donated food must also indicate the presence of common allergens.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be a good condition for us to consider including as well.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Food donation can effectively reduce food waste.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, because donors are afraid of trouble or worry about legal liability due to food safety issues, they would rather throw away the food than donate it.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are still many families in need in our society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, we cannot stop eating because of the fear of choking.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By legislating to exempt food donors who meet food safety and hygiene conditions, we will encourage food donations, reduce food waste, and help families in need.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we must have balance in the new legal framework and not go too far.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the conditions for exempting food donors from liability are too cumbersome, it will increase the cost for potential food donors, which will reduce their willingness to donate and lead them to do the convenient – discarding food.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This leads to us missing the original goal of our legislation and the loss will outweigh the gain.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to exempting food donors from liability through legislation, the government can also implement incentive measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have thought of tax incentives, however, tax incentives have pros and cons.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may inadvertently incentivise people to stockpile or over-purchase, causing unnecessary waste which is exactly the opposite of what we want to achieve.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In general, our legislation needs to balance the interests of food donors and the ultimate beneficiaries.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is the most basic requirement that food donors must comply with food safety regulations when handling food.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The implementation of the Good Samaritan Food Donation legislation can not only reduce food waste, but also help people in need and reduce the burden on the environment. : I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus welcome the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill as I believe that it will further encourage the donation of surplus or unsold food to the needy, tackling the problem of food wastage in a meaningful and purposeful manner through redistribution to communities, families and individuals in need.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding this, I would like to raise some clarifications on the implementation of the proposed section 4 on the waiver of criminal and civil liability.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These non-profit organisations have been at the forefront of addressing food insecurity among our vulnerable communities through ground-up support for food programmes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Food from the Heart, for instance, has been collecting unsold and excess food and groceries from supermarkets and bakeries, and distributing them to those who struggle with food insecurity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their initiatives, such as the School Goodie Bag and Community Food Pack programmes, have benefited the less fortunate families and children in our communities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, GoodHood has revolutionised the concept of neighbourhood sharing through their "GoodHood.SG: Neighbourhood App", encouraging residents to share surplus food and other resources with their residents, with their fellow neighbours in need.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such ground-up approach not only fosters neighbourliness but also encourage Singaporeans to actively participate in the sustainability cause.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My residents in Jalan Kayu have benefited from many of such food donation efforts and I am deeply grateful to them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Like several of my hon Parliamentary colleagues have mentioned, I note that there have been similar legislative efforts by other countries to encourage food donation.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the US, the Federal Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act enacted in 1996 protects donors from liability when donating to non-profit organisations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, Italy’s Good Samaritan Law protects those who donate food in good faith from civil and criminal consequences of their actions and limits their liability arising from food safety rules.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead of legislation, some other countries, such as the UK’s Courtauld Commitment 2030, is a voluntary agreement amongst stakeholders to reduce food wastage by 50% by 2030.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although there may be different approaches to encouraging food donation, many local businesses prefer legislation that reduces their fear of liability and reputation damage, while helping to balance their corporate social responsibility with any potential legal obligations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we move forward, it is thus essential to ensure that the implementation of the Bill can effectively address the concerns raised by potential food donors while ensuring food safety for the recipients.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, I would like to seek clarifications on the administration, imposition of penalties, if any, in serious incidents of breaches and possible mediation process for conditions outlined in section 4 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill provides a waiver of criminal and civil liability for donors of food, under four key conditions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is essential to establish a clear oversight mechanism to ensure that donors adhere to the safety and hygiene protocols required by the Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I hope to understand how the conditions under section 4 will be administered and monitored to ensure compliance by all stakeholders involved.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And will the investigation process into serious breaches be conducted similarly to the process for contamination and gastroenteritis incidents?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that MSE can work with stakeholders to provide training and guidance to potential food donors to help them understand and comply with the requirements of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will also foster a culture of responsibility and encourage ethical behaviour among potential food donors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And will this be a graduated scale of penalties based on the severity of the breach, ranging from minor infractions to serious violations to give assurance to potential food donors?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I would like to also clarify if there will be mediation or resolution processes made available to both donors and recipients to address any grievances or misunderstandings arising from possible disputes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government can consider providing a mediating channel that is reliable for all donors and recipients to address any issues that may arise.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, for small-scale donors who may not have the resources to navigate complex legal disputes, will the Government provide support mechanisms to assist them?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help to foster a more giving and compassionate community in the long term.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through my professional experience, I have witnessed first-hand the shocking amount of perfectly edible food that is discarded into recycling bins.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has reinforced my firm belief that edible food should be redistributed, not recycled.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I fully support this Bill put forth by the hon Member Louis Ng as it will enable more effective redistribution of edible food.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It has been a real privilege to be part of this discussion along with Parliamentary colleagues, Ms Poh Li San and Ms Hany Soh at the onset.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this speech, I will share the various opportunities that this Bill gives rise to.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These opportunities support our nation's efforts to combat food waste and enhance the support for our food-insecure communities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This bodes well for any type of operation as economies of scale are key.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The increase in food sources enables non-profit organisations and social enterprises to achieve the required scale to optimise operations and logistics.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With more food available, food caring organisaions (FCOs) can optimise their processes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They can better match the food with appropriate recipients and plan logistics more effectively.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, with greater food volume, organisations can recover their investments in better infrastructure, such as transportation and storage, improving their overall efficiency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The increase in food sources will also optimise the matching of donors' and donees' preferences.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When businesses, restaurants and individuals donate more surplus food, it increases the potential diversity of food available for redistribution.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This helps organisations have a more consistent and diverse supply to redistribute to those in need.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Combined with digital solutions, the increase in scale can also spark innovations in redistribution methods, such as using technology to track and manage food donations more effectively.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the US, Olio is a food-sharing app that connects neighbours and local businesses with excess food to those nearby who can use it.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such hyperlocal innovations have the potential to enhance community bonds too.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another area of opportunity is the issuance of a quality mark that ensures food is safely and effectively redistributed to those in need.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such certifications and standards typically focus on food safety, operational standards and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, ISO 22000, an international standard that specifies requirements for a food safety management system to ensure that food is safe for consumption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Organisations involved in food rescue and redistribution can obtain this certification to demonstrate their commitment to food safety.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Feeding America has its own set of standards and guidelines for member food banks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Certified members must meet rigorous criteria for food safety, handling and distribution practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For food caring organisations to harness the opportunities presented in this Bill, we need to enable them to take strategic and impactful steps.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are three ways we can do so.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While investing in additional refrigerated vehicles is one option, it may not always be the most efficient and can also contribute to traffic congestion.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, I recommend we focus on creating hyperlocal partnerships and community-based redistribution networks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Community Development Councils (CDCs), organised by districts, are ideally positioned to enable this.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The CDCs could serve as the key node to enable FCOs to operate a hyperlocal hub and spokes redistribution.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Within these hubs, several cold storage facilities can be added to extend the shelf life of perishable items.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By collaborating with FCOs within the CDC districts, the CDCs can enhance existing support to resource low-income families.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This suggestion is built upon our existing weekly food rescue initiative that we have started in Zhenghua.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We collaborated with local supermarkets and wholesalers to gather all unsold food items, which are transported to Zhenghua, where it is distributed among residents.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important to note that we have framed this as a Zhenghua green initiative, where all are welcome to collect the rescued food.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this way, we mobilise all in our community to do our part to reduce food waste.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our on-ground experience shows how hyperlocal initiatives can successfully mobilise volunteers and consistently provided food to the community.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach reduces logistical cost by keeping food redistribution hyperlocal, ensuring food reaches those in need quickly and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, it enhances community resilience and promotes sustainability by fostering a strong network of support within the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By aligning with international methodologies that quantify greenhouse gas emission reductions, these organisations can not only contribute to environmental sustainability but also generate revenue through carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such technologies will enhance transparency and accuracy in measuring their impact, enabling these organisations to capitalise on carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This potential further amplifies the impact of the Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill, fostering a more sustainable and responsible approach to food management in our society.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is a food paradise filled with eateries and restaurants at every corner of our country.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, many of us are unaware of what happens to food that is unsold and how much food is wasted.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: An elephant can weigh up to six tonnes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Here are some facts: one, while food prices are increasing consistently, the options for affordable food supplies for low-income families are still very limited; two, even though SFA has been working hard to meet the "30 by 30" national nutritional goal, a huge quantity of edible food is being thrown away daily; three, 11% of total waste collected in Singapore is food waste and this percentage can be reduced; four, we have a shortage of waste collection workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to ask ourselves why are we throwing away so much food when they can be channelled to feed our under-privileged groups?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This food paradox arises because food is perishable, expensive to store and transport and food that does not look fresh is hard to sell or may even cause health issues.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is not disputed that it is cheaper, more convenient and less risky for food suppliers and restaurants to simply throw away unsold and unconsumed food rather than to donate them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This practice is especially so for well-known food establishments.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is just not worth the risk of damaging an established food company's reputation should the quality and safety of the unconsumed food be compromised in the course of collection and distribution.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As Singaporeans become more affluent, many people tend to take a nonchalant and risk-averse attitude when it comes to wasting food.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, as a small and resource-scarce nation, we must stop the following from increasing – food waste, food costs, food insecurity, manpower needs and carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill will be a good solution.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This legislative amendment can be a significant game-changer in the management of under-utilised food resources and waste reduction while helping low-income families cope with rising food expenses and assisting them in monitoring their nutrition intake.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Presently, there are already several volunteer groups addressing the collection of unconsumed food and redistributing them to various communities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Food from the Heart will collect unsold bread, while Food Rescue Sengkang picks up vegetables and fruits from wholesale markets and food donors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These rescued food items are mostly limited to those that are easier to transport, store, distribute and safe to mark as consumables.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are still plenty of untapped opportunities to rescue unconsumed high-quality foods from restaurants, hotel buffets, supermarkets and so on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If sufficient protection from liability or even benefits are provided for the donation of unconsumed food, more food donors and distribution groups will come onboard.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Such collaboration efforts can potentially create solutions for more ground-up initiatives and attract various communities to work together to reduce food waste and to do good.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We can turn a vicious circle of waste into a virtuous circle of good deeds.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Good Samaritan Food Donation Bill is a good solution.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: But needless to say, a lot more needs to be done in order to reduce significant amounts of food waste and to redistribute edible foods to the under-privileged communities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The logistics is viable because Singapore is small with good transport accessibility to reach anywhere in a short time.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to create awareness of the Good Samaritan Food Bill and hopefully promote an enhanced liability protection extended to food donors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have to encourage lighthouse partners such as the Restaurant Association of Singapore, Singapore Hotel Association and major supermarket chains such as FairPrice and Cold Storage to come onboard as examples for other food suppliers and operators.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We will need to increase the number of volunteers in various localities across Singapore to assist with the collection and distribution roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Key food collection points, donation drop-off nodes and distribution points must be established in various zones across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Volunteer drivers of large vehicles could then ply between the collection nodes and the distribution points while volunteer distributors could help with sorting, cleaning, repacking and distributing the donated foods to beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is also important for the distribution points to be located at convenient and accessible locations for the beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Singapore Armed Forces can also consider activating some National Servicemen to be involved in this process.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have to identify and reach out to more potential beneficiaries who are open to receive donated food and as much as possible, provide fresh and healthy foods.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We also need to help these beneficiaries develop healthy eating habits, especially for growing children.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It would be good for the local Social Service Offices and Family Services Centres work with and to support food donation groups in order to achieve more targeted outreach to low-income families that would benefit from regular food distribution.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to take the following steps to expand donation efforts and deliver donated food to more beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to raise awareness of the Bill and promote enhanced liability protection for food donors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must encourage large partners to participate, such as the Singapore Food and Beverage Industry Association, the Singapore Hotel Association and large supermarket chains, such as NTUC FairPrice and Cold Storage, to set an example for other food suppliers and operators.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to increase volunteers in various districts, including volunteer drivers of large vehicles, to assist in the collection, delivery and distribution of donated food.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Singapore Armed Forces could consider mobilising some National Servicemen to participate in this process.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our residents and volunteers in Sembawang West will also get to benefit more.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Five years ago, my PAP Sembawang West Branch volunteers and I started our "Colourful Food, Vibrant Life" fruits and vegetables distribution programme.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We distributed free fruits and vegetables once a month to our residents staying at our rental block, as well as the 2-room and 3-room blocks.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Apart from a few months during the COVID-19 pandemic, when we had to pause the programme, unfortunately, this programme has brought much joy to both volunteers and beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Thereafter, my branch volunteers will collect one truckload of fruits and vegetables from Fernvale and transport them to Sembawang West rental block.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My volunteers will unload, sort, clean and display the food items at the void deck of the rental block.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some of them will collect on behalf of their neighbours who may be out or unwell.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We started with the intention of reducing food waste, encouraging low-income families to eat more nutritious greens and also helping them reduce their food expenditures.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over time, we got to know the residents better and we forged friendships with them through our chit-chats while they wait in the queue.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Even though they may not be well-endowed or well-educated, many of these residents are very hardworking, warm and down-to-earth.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They are very appreciative of our efforts and we often get warm hugs whenever they see us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are many unexpected beautiful blessings and thank you notes from these distribution sessions are very much appreciated by our volunteers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: During the process, our volunteers, especially the youths, have the opportunity to learn about how we can help under-privileged living in our midst.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is a great eye-opener that brings valuable life education and experiences to these volunteers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In helping senior residents carry their bags of fruits and vegetables to their humble homes, the youths learn to appreciate how fortunate and well-endowed they themselves are.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There is a lot of good done whenever our branch volunteers collaborates with other community or corporate social responsibility groups who have come forward to contribute as well.
